stops.title: Herod's kingdom is divided
stops.summary: Herod the Great dies. Augustus confirms his sons' claims but not as Herod willed them: Archelaus becomes ethnarch (not king) of Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Antipas becomes tetrarch of Galilee and Perea; Philip becomes tetrarch of Gaulanitis, Batanea, Trachonitis and Auranitis. Three Greek cities -- Gaza, Gadara and Hippos -- are cut away and added to the province of Syria.

stops.title: Judea becomes a Roman province
stops.summary: Rome deposes Archelaus and turns his ethnarchy into a province under a prefect (Josephus's own term is "procurator"). Quirinius, governing Syria, conducts a census of Judea. Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus's birth, which Luke and Matthew separately place in King Herod's days; how the two accounts relate is debated. Antipas's and Philip's territories are unaffected. Folded in here: in 2 BC, the district called "Pontus Galaticus," part of the land this map draws as one area with Cappadocia, had already joined the province of Galatia; Cappadocia's own holder does not change.

stops.title: Cappadocia becomes a Roman province
stops.summary: King Archelaus of Cappadocia, summoned to Rome and accused before the Senate, dies there, and his kingdom becomes a province. The Roman historian Tacitus records that two neighboring kings, "Antiochus of Commagene and Philopator of Cilicia," also died about the same time, and that in their countries "the majority of men desired a Roman governor, and the minority a monarch" -- though a translator's note adds that Philopator's own rule covered only a small part of eastern Cilicia, not Cilicia Tracheia. Commagene gets its own Roman governor about this time. The geographer Strabo elsewhere records that Cilicia Tracheia had been part of Archelaus's own former kingdom, but no source says what became of it after his death, so this map shows its holder as unclear from this year.

stops.title: Philip's tetrarchy is absorbed into Syria
stops.summary: Philip dies without an heir after many years as tetrarch. Rome does not appoint a successor tetrarch; his territory is attached to the province of Syria, though its own revenues stay earmarked for it.

stops.title: Caligula makes Agrippa I a king
stops.summary: The new emperor frees his friend Agrippa (Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great) from a Roman prison and makes him king over Philip's former tetrarchy and the neighboring territory of Abilene. Abilene is too small, and its borders too poorly known, to show as its own area on this map, so this change in its ruler appears only in this stop's text.

stops.title: Antipas is banished; his tetrarchy joins Agrippa I's kingdom
stops.summary: Herodias presses her husband Antipas to seek the royal title Caligula gave her brother. Caligula instead banishes Antipas and gives Galilee and Perea to Agrippa I. Folded in here: the previous year, Caligula had made Rhoemetalces II sole ruler over all of Thrace -- a different area -- and had restored the kingdom of Commagene, together with coastal Cilicia Tracheia, to Antiochus IV; within this same year, Caligula took Commagene away from Antiochus IV again, for reasons no source gives, so that area's holder is shown as unclear until Claudius restores it.

stops.title: Agrippa I's kingdom is made whole; new neighbors appear
stops.summary: The new emperor Claudius adds to Agrippa I's kingdom, the Jewish historian Josephus writes, "all that country over which Herod, who was his grandfather, had reigned, that is, Judea and Samaria." At the same time Claudius makes Agrippa I's brother Herod king of Chalcis, capital of the earlier Iturean kingdom, and restores Commagene (with its hold on coastal Cilicia Tracheia) to Antiochus IV, whom Caligula had deprived of it. The Nabataean king Aretas IV dies about this year; Malichus II succeeds him.

stops.title: Agrippa I dies; direct Roman rule returns
stops.summary: Agrippa I dies at Caesarea. Rather than let his young son inherit, Claudius places the whole kingdom -- Judea, Samaria, Galilee, Perea and Philip's former tetrarchy -- under Roman procurators. Folded in here: the previous year, Cassius Dio records that Claudius "reduced the Lycians to servitude because they had revolted and slain some Romans, and he incorporated them in the prefecture of Pamphylia" -- a different area, whose status in the years that follow is itself debated among the sources (see the Lycia area's own note).

stops.title: Agrippa II trades Chalcis for the northern tetrarchy
stops.summary: Claudius, in the twelfth year of his reign, takes Chalcis back from the younger Agrippa (Agrippa I's son, ruling Chalcis since 50) and gives him Philip's former tetrarchy and Abilene instead. Within the next few years, Nero enlarges this grant with the Galilean towns of Tiberias and Tarichaeae (identified with Magdala) and, in Perea, Julias (a different town from Philip's own Bethsaida-Julias in the north) with fourteen villages; Josephus dates this to Nero's first year (AD 54), but the Jewish Encyclopedia reads Agrippa II's own coinage as pointing to AD 61 for this specific addition instead. Neither of these towns is its own area on this map, so this grant does not move any border; it is recorded on the towns themselves. Folded in here: Thrace's status also becomes unclear about this time, disputed between ancient writers; the Thrace area's own note gives both views.

stops.title: Nero frees Achaia from provincial rule
stops.summary: Touring Greece to compete in its games, the emperor Nero grants the province of Achaia its freedom. The Roman biographer Suetonius records that "he presented the entire province with freedom" -- the home of Corinth, Athens, Cenchreae and Nicopolis, among this map's places.

stops.title: Jerusalem falls
stops.summary: After four years of war, Titus's forces take Jerusalem and destroy the Second Temple. The province of Judea is now governed by a legate, with a legion based at Jerusalem, rather than a procurator. Agrippa II, who had sided with Rome, keeps his own separate kingdom. Folded in here: in 63 or 64, Polemon II had given up his client kingdom of eastern Pontus, which the province of Galatia then absorbed as "Pontus Polemoniacus"; this land is not its own area on this map, so the change is named here rather than shown as a border moving (see the Cappadocia area's own note). By this same January, Thrace was already under direct imperial government, settling by fact what ancient writers disputed in principle (see the AD 53 stop).

stops.title: Commagene is annexed; Cilicia is reunited
stops.summary: Vespasian's governor of Syria accuses Antiochus IV of Commagene of plotting with Parthia and annexes his kingdom, including the coastal part of Cilicia Tracheia he held. Lesser Armenia, a small kingdom whose land this map draws together with Cappadocia, is also annexed about this year. The same year, Cilicia Pedias and Cilicia Tracheia are joined again as one province for the first time since Augustus divided them. The Nabataean king Malichus II dies about this year; Rabbel II succeeds him. Cappadocia's own governor from AD 69 on may also have governed Galatia from about this time, though this map keeps them as two areas (see the Cappadocia area's own note).

stops.title: Lycia and Pamphylia become one province
stops.summary: The emperor Vespasian joins Pamphylia with Lycia, which lies to its west, not its south, forming one new province. The Bible scholar Thomas Schreiner notes that Vespasian "detached almost all of Pisidia from Galatia in AD 74" as well; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the same year and records that the cities of southern Pisidia "now ranked as Pamphylian," but no source describes exactly where the new internal line between Pisidia and Galatia ran, so Pisidia's own area stays whole, within Galatia, on this map. Perga's own province changes name and neighbors, from "Galatia" to "Lycia and Pamphylia," though Perga's own ground does not move.

stops.title: Achaia becomes a province again
stops.summary: Suetonius records that Vespasian "made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom," without giving a year for it; this map shows Achaia's status as unclear from Vespasian's accession until his death in 79, the year by which his reversal of Nero's grant was certainly in force.

stops.title: Agrippa II dies; his kingdom joins Syria
stops.summary: The last Herodian ruler dies. Justus of Tiberias, Agrippa II's own secretary, gave this year, read from the lost works of Justus by the ninth-century Byzantine scholar Photius. The historian Nikos Kokkinos defends this date, reading a lead weight found near Tiberias -- on his reading, dated to Agrippa II's own 43rd regnal year (AD 97/98) -- as showing him still reigning shortly before; this reading of the weight's date is disputed among specialists. Other historians instead read Josephus's own wording in the Antiquities to place Agrippa II's death earlier, before AD 93 -- the view of, among others, the standard reference work The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ as revised by Vermes and Millar (1973). His kingdom (Gaulanitis, Batanea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and Abilene) is added to the province of Syria; one modern account notes signs that he had already lost some territory after AD 93.

entities.name: Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea
Roman province of Lycia and Pamphylia
Roman province of Bithynia and Pontus
Roman province of Crete and Cyrene

periods.note: Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch."

Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. How the accounts relate is debated.

periods.ruler: Procurators, e.g. Antonius Felix, Porcius Festus
Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem
periods.note: An administrative upgrade (a legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.

Nero later added the Galilean towns of Tiberias and Tarichaeae (identified with Magdala), and Julias in Perea with fourteen villages, to Agrippa II's kingdom; Josephus dates this to AD 54, but the Jewish Encyclopedia reads Agrippa II's coinage as pointing to AD 61 instead. These are towns, not land of their own, so this area's extent does not change.

periods.ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem
periods.note: An administrative upgrade (a legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
"The country of Zenodorus, lying between Trachonitis and Galilee, and including Paneas and Ulatha, Augustus bestowed on Herod" in 20 BC.

Some historians instead place Agrippa II's death, and so the end of this period, before AD 93, reading the Jewish historian Josephus's own wording in the Antiquities; this is the view of, among others, the standard reference work The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ as revised by Vermes and Millar (1973). This area follows the later, AD 100 dating; see that stop for the sources on both sides.

ISBE's "Trachonitis" entry states that district specifically "was incorporated in the new province of Arabia" in 106, together with the Nabataean kingdom. No source separately confirmed an end point for the other three districts (Gaulanitis, Batanea and Auranitis), so the same year is shown for all four.

ISBE's "Arabia" entry classes the Sinai peninsula with "Arabia Petrea," the region named for Petra, this kingdom's own capital. This area's drawn extent includes Sinai on that geographic basis; no ancient source describes exactly where the line between Arabia and Egypt ran, so a conventional modern approximation is used instead.
Administers the Cilician plain throughout, and administered Philip's former tetrarchy directly for a few years after his death (34-37; Antiquities 18.4.6).
"Quintus Servaeus was appointed to Commagene, now for the first time transferred to praetorian jurisdiction" (Tacitus); Strabo likewise calls it a province by his own day.

Cassius Dio records that Caligula later "restored Commagene to Antiochus [IV], since Gaius [Caligula], though he had himself given him the district, had taken it away again"; the exact year of Caligula's removal is not given.
Administered from Syria throughout; Tarsus sits in this plain.

periods.ruler: Reunited with Cilicia Tracheia as one province

periods.note: Strabo: "Archelaus received, in addition to Cappadocia, Cilicia Tracheia." Tacitus separately records that "Philopator of Cilicia" died in AD 17; the Loeb edition's own note places Philopator's own principality in the east of Cilicia, not Tracheia, so Philopator is not treated as a possible ruler of this area.

Tacitus records a tribe here, the Cietae, as still "subject to Archelaus of Cappadocia" and fighting "the forces of the king" in AD 36, nearly twenty years after Cappadocia itself became a province, leaving how Cilicia Tracheia was actually governed in this span unclear.

Dio gives Antiochus IV only "the coast region of Cilicia," not all of Tracheia, and separately records that in 41 Claudius gave "some land in Cilicia" to Polemon (of the Pontic dynasty) as well, without saying how the two holdings related. Held by Commagene's king, but not part of Commagene's own territory.

periods.ruler: Reunited with Cilicia Pedias as one province
Equestrian governors, the first being Quintus Veranius
periods.note: This area's drawn extent also covers Pontus Galaticus (part of the province of Galatia from 2 BC), Polemon's kingdom of Pontus (a client kingdom until 63 or 64, when it too joined Galatia), and Lesser Armenia (ruled by client kings from AD 38 to 72); none of these three lands is its own area on this map, so they are not shown separately as unclear. This does not change Cappadocia's own holder; see the AD 6 and AD 70 stops for their own changes.

periods.ruler: Consular governors, the first being Gnaeus Pompeius Collega (AD 69)
periods.note: Suetonius records that Vespasian "gave [Cappadocia] a consular governor in place of a Roman knight." Cappadocia and Galatia may have shared one governor from about this time on, which one modern history of the province calls likely, but no ancient source states a merger outright, so the map keeps Cappadocia and Galatia as two areas with their own holders.

Includes Pisidia, Lycaonia (the western part) and Paphlagonia, which had already joined the province of Galatia (Pisidia and Lycaonia in 25 BC on King Amyntas's death; Paphlagonia in 6 BC) before 4 BC. Vespasian detached most of Pisidia to the new province of Lycia and Pamphylia in AD 74; no source describing exactly where that internal line ran was found, so this area is kept whole rather than guessing at a split. Galatia and Cappadocia may have shared one governor from about AD 69 (see the Cappadocia area's own note), though no ancient source states a merger outright, so they stay two areas with their own holders.

Cassius Dio (60.17.3-4) and Tacitus's Histories (2.9, with the Loeb editor's note) disagree on Pamphylia's standing in this span, so it is shown as unclear rather than as part of Galatia. The nearest mapped shape for this period is far larger than Pamphylia's own coastal plain and likely also covers southern Pisidia (part of Galatia throughout); this area's drawn land may therefore include some of Galatia's own territory for these years.

Cassius Dio says Claudius "incorporated them in the prefecture of Pamphylia," not that Lycia became its own province; Suetonius separately records that Vespasian made a province of Lycia, implying it had freedom again by his reign, and the Loeb note to Tacitus's Histories 2.9 states that "Galatia, Pamphylia, and Lycia" formed one province together by AD 69, leaving Lycia's exact status across this span unclear.

This area's drawn extent also covers coastal, western Pontus; ISBE states "the Black Sea littoral as far as Amisus was more or less closely joined with Bithynia in administration." That land is not its own area on this map.
Smith's Dictionary calls Rhoemetalces II "the last native prince," implying one or more earlier rulers in this span whose names were not found.
Smith's Dictionary: "made by Caligula ruler over the whole country" in AD 38.

Smith's Dictionary reports a genuine ancient disagreement: the Eusebian Chronicle dates Thrace's reduction to a province to AD 47, under Claudius, while Suetonius and Eutropius date it to Vespasian's reign (69-79); Smith's own editor favors the later date but allows that Rhoemetalces II may have died around 47, with formal provincial status only delayed. Tacitus's Histories (1.11) independently lists Thrace among the districts "in charge of imperial agents" already in January AD 69, before Vespasian's own reign began.

periods.ruler: Imperial legate of Moesia (governed with Macedonia)

periods.note: Suetonius: on his departure from Greece, Nero "presented the entire province with freedom."

Suetonius records that Vespasian "made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom," but gives no year for this, so the status here is shown as unclear from Vespasian's first full year as emperor until his death in 79, when it is a province again.

periods.ruler: Imperial legate of Moesia (governed with Achaia)
Equestrian prefect; senators barred without the emperor's leave
periods.note: Suetonius: after Cleopatra's death, Augustus "reduced Egypt to the form of a province."
Augustus organized it as one province in AD 10, under an imperial legate residing at Salona on the Dalmatian coast; already under Roman control in the years before that.
